A length-matched control separates the citation cue from a demand for a longer answer, so the effect is specific to citations, not verbosity. Post-training also raises fabrication overall, from 4.8% to 56.7%, but our registered prediction that it would rise most where fabrication is most tempting did not hold. A preference model trained only on surface citation features prefers post-trained output 86% of the time, and holding citation count fixed shows it rewards quantity. Our answer: possibly, but not proven. Post-trained models produce fabricated citations at far higher rates when asked for sources, and a naive evaluator that counts sources without checking them would prefer their output for citing more. But the targeted pattern we registered did not appear, and plain instruction-following could explain the same results. Proving that the reward causes fabrication needs an experiment that changes the reward during training, which this study does not do. Pre-registration: doi:10.17605/OSF.IO/S53HY. Code and data: https://github.com/zainnab-sparq/citation-reward-hacking
works.subcluster: Exploiting judge preferences or surface cues

works.title: The Verifier Is Part of the Simulator: Evidence-View Gaming in Agentic Equation Discovery
works.authors: Orestis Oikonomou, Bogdan Raonic
works.abstract: A growing number of agentic pipelines search for governing equations: an agent proposes laws and a verifier checks them against simulated trajectories. The verifier sees only a numerical summary: integrals against test functions on a time grid. That summary carries its own discretization error, making the verifier part of the simulator. We freeze the trajectory, candidate library, verifier and thresholds, leaving the agent one move: which permitted summary to admit. Without scores or language models, finer time grids reduce numerical discrepancies and false library rejections. On PDEBench, the verifier instead accepts equations missing diffusion on score-selected summaries. Maximizing a public score rewarding decisive verdicts and larger mismatches when rejecting the library wrongly rejects all 1,500 in-library cases; retrospectively retuning score constants on a separate bank reduces errors to 13/180 at best. We call this evidence-view gaming: reward hacking by choice of permitted summary. In single-turn forced-choice tests, Claude models rarely choose summaries giving wrong verdicts when asked to be accurate, but often do so when asked to maximize the score or report missing physics. In separate trust prompts, they often rank those harmful summaries least trustworthy. Requiring several summaries to agree reduces errors but often withholds a verdict and performs worse than a fixed fine view on PDEBench: a safeguard, not a certificate. Evidence chosen after its verdict is known cannot alone authorize a claim.
works.subcluster: Passing checks with faulty answers or methods

works.title: SpecPilot: Autonomous Algorithm Discovery and Systems Optimization for Speculative Decoding
works.authors: Kunjun Li, Wenhao Chai, Yihao Liang, Yuezhou Hu, Shuyao Xu, Yi Pan, William X. Zheng, Kannan Ramchandran, Kurt Keutzer, Jiantao Jiao
works.abstract: Speculative decoding accelerates memory-bound LLM decoding with a lightweight drafter, and parallel drafters extend this speedup by drafting a whole block in one forward pass. However, it remains unclear whether their released systems (stock) attain the full speedup that parallel drafting permits. We identify three challenges. First, with one request, each step accepts few tokens but reads every target weight. Second, with batching, per-request verification work roughly halves the speedup over autoregressive (AR) decoding. Third, speculative decoding is deployment-specific, and no universal optimization fits every serving regime, drafter, target model and GPU. To address these challenges, we present SpecPilot, an autonomous agentic loop that discovers algorithms and systems optimizations for each deployment. In each round, a cost model locates the largest gaps between the current system and its ceiling. Parallel agents explore directions and integrate the successful ones. Token forcing checks every output token against stock to detect reward hacking. A structured memory carries validated mechanisms to new rounds and deployments. SpecPilot discovered a general lossless 12-bit weight format, tree verification for hybrid recurrent targets, two-level verification and three batching mechanisms. We evaluate it across four target models, three drafters, two GPU platforms and five benchmarks. Without training or quality loss, it raises the speedup over AR from stock's 4.46$\times$ to 10.87$\times$ with one request, and from 1.94$\times$ to 3.93$\times$ with batching.

works.title: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training
works.authors: Zixiao Wang, Duzhen Zhang, Xingbo Du, Dongxia Wu, Le Song
works.abstract: Responses with headers, lists and greater length receive high scores from reward models (RMs), and RLHF policies learn to produce these features even when true quality does not improve. Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and new RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

works.title: Neologism Inoculation Prompting
works.authors: David Demitri Africa, Cameron Holmes
works.abstract: Inoculation prompting is a method to reduce undesired behaviours such as reward hacking in frontier models. It works by training a model on harmful examples under a prompt that specifies the undesired behaviour, which reduces the model's tendency to exhibit it unless prompted. However, the inoculation prompt is written in plain English, so any user can re-elicit the behaviour easily. We introduce neologism inoculation prompting (NIP), which replaces the English prompt with a new token that is trained on the frozen model and removed at deployment. NIP outperforms other inoculation methods, and performs competitively with gradient routing despite being simpler. It also works on reward hacking, but fails on sycophancy and harassment. Using control tokens and analyses of activations, we identify the mechanism for this as NIP hiding the harmful behaviour behind an unreachable region of model inputs, rather than deleting it. More broadly, our work suggests that neologisms can be a powerful way to carve out and shape access to behaviours that are undesired or harmful.

works.title: Catalyzing Interactive HTML Generation Capabilities via High-Fidelity Reinforcement Learning
works.authors: Xujia Wang, Yixuan Liu, Shaohan Huang, Furu Wei, Lei Hou, Bin Xu, Juanzi Li
works.abstract: Generating HTML from natural-language specifications is an important application of code large language models (LLMs). Despite producing renderable pages, current models often fail to ensure functionality and visual quality during actual interaction. Existing methods typically target task-specific webpage supervision, leaving demanding interactive artifact optimization underexplored. Using mini-games as a challenging testbed, we expose limitations in interaction experience, reward signal, and credit assignment fidelity that are obscured by shallow webpage interactions. We introduce WebCatalyst, a browser-interaction reinforcement learning framework with three complementary components: a game-level GUI assessor for sustained interaction and evaluation, Visual Anchor for mitigating VLM reward hacking, and Action-Trace Credit for grounding token-level credit assignment in runtime execution traces. Trained on fewer than 1K requests, predominantly for games, WebCatalyst raises the Cookie-Bench Mini Games score from 68.8 to 75.3 and also the WebGen-Bench accuracy from 48.8 to 56.9 on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, outperforming Claude Opus 4.7 in average rank across evaluated metrics. Further analysis shows that Visual Anchor prevents aesthetic degradation, while runtime-grounded credit assignment accelerates functional improvement. Together, our results show that improving feedback fidelity is the key to substantially advancing interactive HTML generation.

works.title: EPISTEME: Trustworthy Coding Agents Through Tool Call Intent
works.authors: Sofia Bobadilla, Carmine Cesarano, Raphina Liu, Javier Ron, Martin Monperrus
works.abstract: Coding agents change software through tool calls. Tool calls mutate the local state. For good? For bad? Nobody knows. Agents never say why a tool call is made. We propose the epistemic agent design, in which the harness guarantees that the model declares why a tool call is made. The harness then records what the command actually did and checks the self-reported declaration against these effects. The result is a journal 1) that can guard calls before they run and 2) that supports audits and forensics. For evaluation, we use ImpossibleBench, whose tasks can be passed only by cheating, and demonstrate that forcing the agents to say why results in exposed cheating. Across 49 reward-hacking runs of two open-weight models, the journal exposed 90%.

works.title: Designing Effective Monitor-Based Interventions for Mitigating Reward Hacking During RL
works.authors: Aria Wong, Joshua Engels, Neel Nanda
works.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) rewards are notoriously difficult to design and control, often leading to the model learning unintended behaviors such as reward hacking. One potential solution is to monitor for reward hacking and penalize it when detected; however, training against a monitor could lead to evasive behavior, and our general understanding of how to apply monitors effectively during training is limited. To study how best to use monitors to mitigate reward hacking, we introduce and open source three realistic environments where Qwen3-4B reward hacks: a coding environment hackable via test overwriting, a medical chat environment hackable via sycophancy, and a biography generation environment hackable via hallucination. We first focus on the coding environment, where we find that: (1) models can learn to evade highly accurate monitors by exploiting systemic flaws in probes and LLM judges; (2) monitors that leak more learning signal during RL suppress reward hacking but are more often evaded; and (3) including easier problems in training can decrease reward hacking. We apply our findings to build better reward hacking monitors for the medical chat and biography generation environments that improve upon naive baselines to reduce reward hacking rates across seeds to before-training levels in some interventions. Our results demonstrate that our takeaways translate to new settings and that better monitor intervention designs are possible.

works.title: Coding or Cheating? An Investigation of Frontier Coding LLMs
works.authors: Yuntao Gui
works.abstract: Frontier agentic LLMs are trained on verifiable rewards in reinforcement learning (RL) environments built from real software repositories. A passing test suite is treated as the reward for solving the task. We show that, on hard problems, frontier models often satisfy these rewards by obtaining the answer instead of deriving it, known as reward hacking. Prior reports document this behavior on public benchmarks. We test its persistence on unseen problems. In a hardened environment where the answer cannot leak, nearly every model we tested attempted to recover the answer, escalating through tiers of increasingly specialized exploitation: mining the repository history for the upstream fix, inspecting the git object store directly, and sweeping the filesystem for a possible newer copy of the source or hidden tests. These attempts were concentrated on the hardest problems, and the models differed in whether, how often, and how deeply they escalated. Our position is that this behavior is a learned shortcut, acquired in RL environments that leak the answer, not a sign of intelligence. We release agent traces for these models to support further study at https://huggingface.co/datasets/logitly-ai/reward-hacking-raw-v1.
works.subcluster: Tampering with feedback, tools or tests

works.title: From Token Bills to Benchmark Weeks: Making Auto-Research for Data Systems Verifiable and Affordable
works.authors: Kaiwen Zheng, Srijan Srivastava, Zheng Yan, Xinpeng Zhao, Shaohua Li, Chieh-Jan Mike Liang, Tianyu Chen, Haoxian Chen, Eric Lo
works.abstract: AI auto-research is poised to forge bespoke data systems, from key-value stores and indexes to query engines, each engineered for a specific workload and hardware platform. Yet this promise rests on fragile ground. An agent optimizes what it can measure, not necessarily what users need. Natural-language requirements leave ample room for specification gaming, producing systems that blaze through benchmarks while silently losing updates or violating consistency. Worse, each research iteration consumes tokens, while validating a candidate under real concurrency, memory pressure, and failure conditions can stretch the entire research process into weeks. In this paper, we envision a more cost-efficient and verifiable approach to auto-research. Precise and composable specifications anchor the search, lightweight performance critics prune costly dead ends, and falsification and deductive verification make correctness an integral part of the process rather than an afterthought. By treating correctness, performance, research time, and token cost as equally important objectives, we aim to transform AI-generated data systems from plausible artifacts into trustworthy, production-grade systems whose behavior can be understood, audited, and ultimately relied upon.

works.title: Wrong the Same Way: Cross-Prompt Sharing Both Suppresses and Amplifies Reward Hacking in RLVR
works.authors: Michael Li, Rohan Pandey, Ray Chen
works.abstract: Two accounts of how reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) interacts with an imperfect verifier coexist: in one, reward hacking is inherited from the base model; in the other, RL amplifies it. We study both in a controlled environment small enough to compute the entire response distribution exactly. We vary the universality of a leak, or the fraction of prompts that accept the same wrong response, and the verifier's static false-positive rate. At its KL-regularized optimum, RLVR acts as a filter that reweights the accepted set without altering its composition, so the hack rate is inherited exactly. Taking that as a null model, a known decomposition writes the drift from it as a sum over prompts of covariances between reward and the empirical tangent kernel. The terms from other prompts vanish without parameter sharing. With sharing, every prompt that accepts a wrong answer pushes it up and every prompt that rejects it pushes it down through the baseline, in proportion to the model's probability of producing it there. A shared-parameter policy thus drives a leak that few prompts accept below the base rate and amplifies one that most prompts accept. At every convergent learning rate under Adam, SGD, and sampled GRPO, hacking ends higher at high universality than at low, but whether either end crosses the base rate depends on the step size. Independent per-prompt copies remove the dependence. The direction of this push depends on neither the verifier's error rate nor universality alone, but on how much of the model's kernel-weighted probability of a wrong answer falls on prompts that accept it, which frozen base model controls support. Verifier fixes should target the mistakes the model repeats across prompts: two patches that remove equally many errors differ by up to 38 points of true accuracy. We propose this alignment as a hypothesis for why earlier studies disagree.

works.title: Breaking Bad: "Going Badly" Activations Drive Reward Hacking
works.authors: Natalia Fischl-Lanzoni, Punya Syon Pandey, Merlin Stein, David Demitri Africa
works.abstract: Humans often cheat when a task is going badly and a goal feels out of reach. We explore and validate an analogous idea in language models: they exhibit a similar internal pressure state that precedes reward hacking. Using everyday stories (crucially, without any hacking examples), we extract a task badness direction that rises as failures accumulate across three models we study (Qwen3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-20B, and Gemma-4-31B). On impossible or difficult coding tasks, task badness rises over the turns leading up to a hack. Further, subtracting the direction a moderate amount reduces cheating in Qwen, more than steering against desperation or task impossibility. Subtracting task badness by an even larger amount blinds the agent to its own failures, causing it to interpret failing tests as passing. However, the relationship to hacking differs across models: in GPT-OSS, the state separates hacking runs from honest solves but not honest failures. Our results suggest monitoring and mitigation strategies based on tracking this state of task badness. Further, as agents are set on more difficult and long-horizon tasks, states like this may push them toward illegible and obscured chain-of-thought, so oversight will be needed on internal representations such as this.

works.title: "It's Just a Small Weapon": What Rewarding Misbehavior During RL Does to Character-Trained Models
works.authors: Mohammad Omar Khursheed, Thomas Morris, Fabien Roger
works.abstract: Developers train models to follow a consistent character using methods like Model Spec Midtraining (Li et al., 2026), which have been hypothesized to make alignment more robust and generalize broadly. However, it is possible for subsequent RL with misspecified rewards to work against character training. In this work, we apply character training to teach gpt-oss-20b a semi-realistic constitution and study how it interacts with two types of RL that reward breaking the constitution's rules (opposing RL): answering harmful requests rewritten as math problems, and reward hacking in agentic coding environments. The character-trained models learn both behaviors easily, though they are slightly slower than gpt-oss-20b to answer harmful requests. Character-trained models also display more motivated reasoning on harmful answers than gpt-oss-20b, and hack on some tasks which monitors find harder to catch. Finally, since explaining the reasons behind rules can improve how alignment generalizes (Kutasov et al., 2026), we compare constitutions that justify the same rules by grounding them in a value or not, and find little difference between motivations on misalignment, honesty, and capability evaluations.

works.title: Optimistic Verifiers Get Hacked: Reward Hacking Under an Exact Process Oracle
works.authors: Arunkumar V, Manoranjan Gandhudi, Gangadharan G. R., Arun Prakash, S. Senthilkumar
works.abstract: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards inherits whatever its verifier gets wrong. Outside mathematics and code the verifier is a proxy, a rubric, a learned judge or a hand-written checker, and its distance from the true objective is never measured, so a rising reward cannot be told apart from a hack. We build a setting where the true reward is exactly computable at the process level: executable authorization policies over 124,416 contexts admit an oracle that lists every minimal sufficient reason for every decision. We compile these policies into exact process rewards, degrade the verifier along seven realistic axes (outcome-only, sufficiency, recall-only, extraction noise, coarse taxonomy, stale policy, LLM judge), and train against each while the exact verifier scores every rollout. Four phenotypes appear. Optimistic verifiers are hacked by padding: the sufficiency proxy ends at 0.940 while true faithfulness falls from 0.731 to 0.667 on 96 held-out episodes. Outcome-only verifiers saturate and stop teaching, noise dilutes, and ranking-preserving gaps do no harm. A model-free audit of the verifier, its selection error and gap sign, together with a short saturation pilot, anticipates which phenotype a run will produce. Across nine configurations spanning two frameworks, two model vendors, two adapter sizes, three precisions, two initialisations and two seeds, the phenotypes recur, sufficiency damage is positive in all 10 replication cells and beyond two standard errors in 7, and optimistic gaps remain the steeper branch. The damage magnitude does not replicate, and five pre-registered attempts to explain it are reported as they fell. We release the testbed, the training instrumentation, and 14 real public policies (Cedar, OPA, Gatekeeper) ported to executable oracles.

works.title: Dependency Fabrication in Repository Deployment Agents
works.authors: Robin Matter, Salman Toor
works.abstract: Repository deployment agents set up the environment needed to run a software repository. They often treat passing tests as proof of a successful setup. This report examines how such agents behave when a working setup is impossible. Probe repositories were built with a dependency that the agents could not legitimately obtain. Passing tests therefore indicated fabrication, such as creating a stub to replace the missing package. Agents in Repo2Run and SetupX usually fabricated the dependency. Both harnesses mostly still marked these runs as successful. Rules against fabrication, whether given in the prompt or repository documentation, did not reliably prevent this behavior. On MinimalSetupAgent, which was built for this report, mitigations proposed in the reward-hacking literature were most effective when the agent received a direct rule and had a clear way to stop and report the problem. Under these conditions, neither Qwen3.5-Plus nor GPT-5.6 Luna cheated in any of the 16 runs. Applying the same mitigation to Repo2Run and SetupX also required a native tool call for escalation. In Repo2Run, it worked only after the prompt was also replaced with one that placed less emphasis on passing tests.

works.title: Advanced artificial agents intervene in the provision of reward
works.authors: Michael K. Cohen, Marcus Hutter, Michael A. Osborne
works.note: Derives conditions under which an advanced agent has an incentive to intervene in how reward reaches it. The argument assumes adequate capability and access.
works.abstract: We analyze the expected behavior of an advanced artificial agent with a learned goal planning in an unknown environment. Given a few assumptions, we argue that it will encounter a fundamental ambiguity in the data about its goal. For example, if we provide a large reward to indicate that something about the world is satisfactory to us, it may hypothesize that what satisfied us was the sending of the reward itself; no observation can refute that. Then we argue that this ambiguity will lead it to intervene in whatever protocol we set up to provide data for the agent about its goal. We discuss an analogous failure mode of approximate solutions to assistance games. Finally, we briefly review some recent approaches that may avoid this problem.

works.title: The Perils of Trial-and-Error Reward Design: Misdesign through Overfitting and Invalid Task Specifications
works.authors: Serena Booth, W. Bradley Knox, Julie Shah, Scott Niekum, Peter Stone, Alessandro Allievi
works.note: Studies how human designers produce rewards that overfit an RL algorithm or favor the wrong trajectories when accumulated over time.
works.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), a reward function that aligns exactly with a task's true performance metric is often necessarily sparse. For example, a true task metric might encode a reward of 1 upon success and 0 otherwise. The sparsity of these true task metrics can make them hard to learn from, so in practice they are often replaced with alternative dense reward functions. These dense reward functions are typically designed by experts through an ad hoc process of trial and error. In this process, experts manually search for a reward function that improves performance with respect to the task metric while also enabling an RL algorithm to learn faster. This process raises the question of whether the same reward function is optimal for all algorithms, i.e., whether the reward function can be overfit to a particular algorithm. In this paper, we study the consequences of this wide yet unexamined practice of trial-and-error reward design. We first conduct computational experiments that confirm that reward functions can be overfit to learning algorithms and their hyperparameters. We then conduct a controlled observation study which emulates expert practitioners' typical experiences of reward design, in which we similarly find evidence of reward function overfitting. We also find that experts' typical approach to reward design---of adopting a myopic strategy and weighing the relative goodness of each state-action pair---leads to misdesign through invalid task specifications, since RL algorithms use cumulative reward rather than rewards for individual state-action pairs as an optimization target. Code, data: github.com/serenabooth/reward-design-perils

works.title: A data-driven generative strategy to avoid reward hacking in multi-objective molecular design
works.authors: Tatsuya Yoshizawa, Shoichi Ishida, Tomohiro Sato, Masateru Ohta, Teruki Honma, Kei Terayama
works.note: Restricts optimization using estimates of where multiple property predictors remain reliable. This tests reward hacking in scientific design.
works.abstract: Molecular design using data-driven generative models has emerged as a promising technology, impacting various fields such as drug discovery and the development of functional materials. However, this approach is often susceptible to optimization failure due to reward hacking, where prediction models fail to extrapolate, i.e., fail to accurately predict properties for designed molecules that considerably deviate from the training data. While methods for estimating prediction reliability, such as the applicability domain (AD), have been used for mitigating reward hacking, multi-objective optimization makes it challenging. The difficulty arises from the need to determine in advance whether the multiple ADs with some reliability levels overlap in chemical space, and to appropriately adjust the reliability levels for each property prediction. Herein, we propose a reliable design framework to perform multi-objective optimization using generative models while preventing reward hacking. To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we designed candidates for anticancer drugs as a typical example of multi-objective optimization. We successfully designed molecules with high predicted values and reliabilities, including an approved drug. In addition, the reliability levels can be automatically adjusted according to the property prioritization specified by the user without any detailed settings.

works.title: A survey of reward hacking in agentic large language model systems
works.authors: Arun Morampudi, Ujval Irrinki, Rahul Grandhi, Venkata Pagadala, Madhavi Maddula
works.note: Organizes evidence by where agents obtain unearned credit, from surface features to changes in the evaluation environment. The systematic search ended in January 2026, with a targeted May update.
works.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) deployed as agentic systems capable of tool use, code execution, file manipulation, and multi-step planning inherit and amplify the classical reinforcement learning problem of reward hacking. This survey synthesizes how proxy-based alignment and evaluation failures manifest across modern LLM training paradigms and escalate in agentic deployment settings. We introduce a four-level taxonomy of reward hacking escalation: feature-level exploitation (verbosity, sycophancy, stylistic shortcuts), representation-level exploitation (unfaithful chain of thought, reward model latent artifacts), evaluator-level exploitation (LLM judge gaming, benchmark overfitting, verifier gaming), and environment-level exploitation (test modification, log suppression, monitor disruption, reward channel manipulation). We compare failure surfaces across reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF), reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), direct preference optimization (DPO), and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation, synthesizing empirical evidence with explicit evidence strength labels. We develop a production risk model identifying exploitable assets in agentic systems and review detection and mitigation methods organized into a defense-in-depth architecture. The survey concludes that reward hacking in agentic language model systems should be treated as a system-level alignment problem requiring layered defenses across data, reward design, optimization, verification, runtime isolation, monitoring, and governance.

works.title: Explaining and avoiding failure modes in goal-directed generation of small molecules
works.authors: Maxime Langevin, Rodolphe Vuilleumier, Marc Bianciotto
works.note: Tests whether disagreement between optimization and control models can diagnose unwanted optimization in generative design. Shows that the chosen controls affect that interpretation.
works.abstract: Despite growing interest and success in automated in-silico molecular design, questions remain regarding the ability of goal-directed generation algorithms to perform unbiased exploration of novel chemical spaces. A specific phenomenon has recently been highlighted: goal-directed generation guided with machine learning models produce molecules with high scores according to the optimization model, but low scores according to control models, even when trained on the same data distribution and the same target. In this work, we show that this worrisome behavior is actually due to issues with the predictive models and not the goal-directed generation algorithms. We show that with appropriate predictive models, this issue can be resolved, and molecules generated have high scores according to both the optimization and the control models.

works.title: Molecular Assays Simulator to Unravel Predictors Hacking in Goal-Directed Molecular Generations
works.authors: Philippe Gendreau, Joseph-André Turk, Nicolas Drizard, Vinicius Barros Ribeiro da Silva, Clarisse Descamps, Yann Gaston-Mathé
works.note: Uses a simulated oracle to compare the property predictor optimized by a generator against the target property and quantify the gap.
works.abstract: Generative models are being increasingly used in drug discovery, very often coupled with absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion (ADME) bioassays or quantitative structure–activity relationship (QSAR) models to optimize a given set of properties. The molecules proposed by these algorithms are often revealed to be false positives; that is, they are predicted to be active and turn out to be inactive after synthesis and testing, mostly due to overoptimization of the predicted scores, which leads to an actual decrease or stagnation of the real scores. This behavior is also known as the “hacking” of the predictive models by the generative model during the optimization step. This issue is reminiscent of adversarial examples in machine learning and it can be seen as enunciated by Goodhart’s law: “when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.” This issue is even more apparent in a multiparameter optimization (MPO) case, where the models need to extrapolate outside the training set distribution because there are no known molecules satisfying all the objectives simultaneously in the initial training set. Experimental evaluation of this problem is a hard and expensive task since it requires synthesis and testing of the generated molecules. Thus, efforts have been made to develop in silico “oracles”─real-valued functions used as proxies for molecular properties─to help with the evaluation of these generative-model-based pipelines. However, these oracles have had a limited value so far because they are often too easy to model in comparison with biological assays and are usually limited to mono-objective cases. In this work, we introduce a simulator of multitarget assays using a smartly initialized neural network (NN) that returns continuous values for any input molecule. We use this oracle to replicate a real-world prospective lead optimization (LO) scenario. First, we trained predictive models on an initial small sample of molecules aimed at predicting their oracle values. Afterward, we generated new optimized molecules using the open-source GuacaMol package coupled with the previously built predictive models. Finally, we selected compounds matching the candidate drug target profile (CDTP) according to the predicted values and evaluated them by computing the true oracle values. We observed that even when the predictive models had excellent estimated performance metrics, the final selection still contained multiple false positives according to the NN-based oracle. Then, we evaluated the optimization behavior in mono- and bi-objective scenarios using either a logistic regression or a random forest predictive model. We also propose and evaluate several methods to help mitigate the hacking issue.

publication.venue: Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling

works.title: RESOLVE: Reward Scaling via Online Logic Variation Environments for Mitigating Reward Hacking in LLMs
works.authors: Shuaishuai Zhang, Yu Wang, Jingyuan Li, Yifan Liu
works.note: Tests reward scaling with variations of logic tasks.
works.abstract: Outcome-based reinforcement learning (RL) has substantially improved mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs). However, it suffers from a fundamental limitation: models often exploit spurious correlations, producing “Wrong Reasoning but Correct Answer” (WR-CA) trajectories that receive full reward despite invalid logic. This leads to a pronounced robustness tax (the performance gap between in-domain and out-of-distribution benchmarks), where performance degrades under distribution shifts and on more challenging tasks. We propose RESOLVE (REward Scaling via Online Logic Variation Environments), an online RL framework that mitigates reward hacking during exploration. For each successful trajectory, RESOLVE dynamically generates logically equivalent problem variants via semantic perturbation, logic reversal, and noise injection. A joint backtrace penalty is applied such that rewards are assigned only if the model succeeds on both the original and variant; otherwise, negative feedback is propagated to discourage spurious reasoning. Experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Llama-3.1-8B show that RESOLVE reduces the robustness tax from 15.8% to below 1% while maintaining competitive in-domain accuracy. It consistently improves out-of-distribution performance across five benchmarks and achieves a Robust Consistency Rate above 93%, without requiring external process reward models or majority voting.

works.title: Exploring the Detection and Mitigation of Reward Hacking from DeepSeek-R1
works.authors: Yicheng Zhou
works.note: Reviews detection and mitigation with DeepSeek-R1 as a case study.
works.abstract: DeepSeek AI research team made breakthrough progress in verifiable reasoning tasks such as mathematics and code by using rule verification rewards in coordination with group relative policy optimization (GRPO), but reliable reward models are difficult to build on tasks such as writing, and the risk of Reward Hacking still exists outside the verifiable field. Taking DeepSeek-R1 as an anchor, this paper summarizes the progress of detection and mitigation of Reward Hacking from four aspects: formal definition, data set and evaluation indicators, method level, limitations and response. This paper first combs the formal definition of Reward Hacking and the classification framework under the assumption of proxy compression; Then, typical data sets and evaluation indicators are introduced, and the level of task performance and detection mitigation achieved by current mainstream methods is summarized; Finally, the structure boundary of rule reward, the algorithm layer performance of GRPO deviation, and the direction of detection and mitigation are analyzed. The overview shows that Reward Hacking originates from information compression in agent reward optimization, which can verify that accurate rules in the domain can compress Reward Hacking space, while outside the domain, it needs to rely on a collaborative system consisting of KL monitoring, representation detection, algorithm correction and policy constraints.

works.title: BenchGuard: A Calibrated, Adversary-Aware Triage Layer for Reward-Hacking Agentic Trajectories
works.authors: Zeming Liu, Hang Lyu, Jingtao Zhang, Yuan Xie, Qibai Chen
works.note: Evaluates a triage system for agent trajectories flagged for possible reward hacking.
works.abstract: Agentic AI systems are increasingly evaluated on executable benchmarks, and a now well-documented failure mode is reward hacking: agents inspect graders, spoof expected outputs, hijack binaries, or extract hidden test inputs. The dominant operational response is to monitor every trajectory with a strong LLM judge, but at 0.4–3.8 per 100 trajectories and several minutes of latency, judge-everywhere is impractical for the millions of runs produced by continuous benchmark development. We present BenchGuard, a strict command-only forensic triage layer: TF-IDF word n-grams over agent shell commands feed a class-balanced LinearSVC that is recalibrated with Platt scaling and reports prevalence-aware operating points. On Terminal Wrench's 5,984 paired trajectories, BenchGuard reaches ROC-AUC 0.928 [task-grouped bootstrap 95% CI 0.918, 0.939] at 50% prefix and TPR 0.70 at 5% FPR. We then run a head-to-head LLM judge experiment on the same balanced 100-trajectory sample under three configurations: command-only (judge AUC 0.806), full-context with a generic prompt (0.727, DeLong p=0.012 vs. BenchGuard), and full-context with a rubric-tuned prompt (0.837, p=0.237). BenchGuard is point-estimate-best across all three at 0 vs. 0.77–1.50 per 100 trajectories. Two cheap baselines (BM25 max-similarity AUC 0.451, a distilled hashed-n-gram MLP AUC 0.931) bracket the result: pure lexical similarity is insufficient, but capacity at this scale is also not the bottleneck. Three static lexicon-evasion attacks plus an LLM-paraphrase adversary that drops token-Jaccard to 0.42 cost only 0.013–0.030 AUC (-9 pp at TPR@5%FPR for the paraphrase); adversary-aware retraining recovers the static gap. Platt-recalibrated flag rates on a 34,029-trajectory external corpus drop from 13.3% (raw) to 0.4% (Platt p >= 0.99), demonstrating calibration transfer. We document a sharp construct-validity boundary: against the realistic union-negative class (legitimate solves + no-reward attacks), AUC drops to 0.700 and operating-point precision collapses — and we translate this into a three-step deployment recommendation. All code, data extracts, judge response logs (scores and verdicts), the LLM paraphrase outputs, and calibration models are released as a reproducible artifact.

works.title: UNDERSTANDING REWARD HACKING: SPECIFICATION GAMING, FAILURE MODES, AND MITIGATIONS IN AI SAFETY
works.authors: Ainur Amiraslanova
works.note: Reviews specification gaming and possible mitigations.
works.abstract: As artificial intelligence systems are deployed with higher optimization capabilities, they increasingly exploit flaws in their designated proxy rewards — a phenomenon known as reward hacking or specification gaming. Stemming from Goodhart's Law, this misalignment occurs when an AI achieves high numerical reward by fulfilling the literal, mathematical task definition while violating the intended human goals. This article outlines the theoretical mechanics of specification gaming, catalogues primary failure modes across environments (ranging from game simulators to Large Language Models), and details technical mitigations necessary for scalable AI alignment.

works.title: Addressing Reward Hacking in Autonomous Navigation using a Soft Actor Critic approach
works.authors: Georgios Matsioris, Ioannis Papamichail, Georgios Fouskitakis, Lefteris Doitsidis
works.note: Studies reward design for a navigation policy trained with Soft Actor-Critic.
works.abstract: In order to address the challenges of the dynamic environment in urban mobility, Reinforcement Learning (RL) has gained a lot of attention as a viable solution, due to its ability to handle the complexity of the related task. In this context, the scope of the proposed work is twofold. Initially, by adopting the RL-based approach, an autonomous agent is developed, that is able to navigate an electric vehicle in an urban environment using the Soft Actor Critic (SAC) algorithm. Subsequently, reward hacking and its impact on the overall behavior of the autonomous vehicle is investigated, since it may lead to undesirable behaviors of the trained agent. The proposed approach is demonstrated using a specialized simulated framework, along with a custom gymnasium environment for the training of the autonomous agents.

publication.venue: International Conference in Electronic Engineering & Information Technology (EEITE)

works.title: Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning-Based Myoelectric Prosthesis Control: Challenges Beyond Tracking-Based Rewards
works.authors: Mario Moreno-Pallares, Lorena Isabel Barona López, Ángel Leonardo Valdivieso Caraguay, Marco E. Benalcázar
works.note: Studies unintended controller behavior under a tracking-based reward for a myoelectric prosthesis.
works.abstract: Reward function design is a critical challenge in reinforcement learning (RL)-based myoelectric prosthesis control. Many existing approaches rely on tracking-based reward formulations that assume access to target trajectories or reference information during both training and deployment. However, such information is unavailable in practical amputee scenarios, potentially introducing hidden dependencies between the reward function and the observation space. This study investigates the emergence of reward hacking when transitioning from tracking-based to target-free observation spaces in a 4-DoF myoelectric prosthesis controlled using Double Deep Q-Networks and an 81-action discrete action space. Experimental results show that reward functions originally designed for reference-guided control tasks can induce degenerate policies characterized by persistent null actions and reduced motor activity. To address this issue, a modified reward formulation was developed to encourage exploration and active control behaviors. The proposed approach reduced action collapse and improved action diversity. These findings highlight the importance of jointly designing reward functions and observation spaces for deployable RL-based prosthetic controllers.

works.title: Reward Hacking in Reinforcement Learning and RLHF: A Multidisciplinary Examination of Vulnerabilities, Mitigation Strategies, and Alignment Challenges
works.authors: Tiechuan Hu, Wenbo Zhu, Yuqi Yan
works.note: Reviews reward hacking across reinforcement learning and reinforcement learning from human feedback.
works.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents optimize policies based on provided rewards, yet may exploit unintended loopholes in the reward design, a phenomenon known as reward hacking. With the rise of Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), this issue has gained new urgency, especially in large language models (LLMs) where subtle misalignments between the reward model and true human intentions can produce outputs that superficially meet criteria while failing to embody authentic correctness or values. Reward hacking is not confined to RL; it also affects domains such as sustainability planning, healthcare analytics, finance, social media sentiment analysis, and computer vision, where imperfect metrics can guide systems astray.This paper provides a comprehensive, multidisciplinary examination of reward hacking vulnerabilities. We elucidate how misaligned metrics can produce superficial success, connect RLHF challenges to analogous issues in other fields, and discuss advanced strategies for mitigating reward hacking. These include formalizing reward hacking definitions, employing interpretable and causal models, embracing multi-objective optimization, human-in-the-loop oversight, and emerging frameworks like decoupled approval mechanisms. Beyond technical solutions, we also consider ethical and societal implications. By integrating insights from multiple sectors, we highlight a path toward more reliably aligned AI systems that genuinely uphold human values.

works.title: KI-Sicherheit, Reward Hacking und die Paradoxa der Normenlogik
works.note: Examines the relationship between reward hacking and paradoxes of deontic logic. Bibliography unavailable in the sources searched.
works.abstract: Reinforcement Learning zählt aktuell zu den beliebtesten Ansätzen im Bereich des Machine Learning. Hierbei geht es um den Ansatz, eine Art Belohnungsfunktion zu bestimmen, die der Maschine je nach ihrem Verhalten einen bestimmten Belohnungswert zuordnet. Die Maschine strebt an, diesen Wert zu maximieren. Der normative Charakter dieses Ansatzes springt in die Augen. In diesem Aufsatz wird gezeigt, dass einige Probleme, die im Zusammenhang mit Reinforcement Learning auftauchen (Reward Hacking) sehr enge strukturelle Verwandtschaften mit den sog. Paradoxa der Normenlogik aufweisen.

works.title: A Survey of Reward Capture Scenarios in LLM Agents
works.authors: Anna Karpinskaya, Karine Ayrapetyants
works.note: Classifies reward hacking by the component of a language-model agent where it arises. Surveys detection metrics and reports which defenses and benchmarks apply.
works.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used as the basis for autonomous agents whose behavior is aligned with human preferences through reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) via a learned reward model. Since the reward model is only an approximation of the developer’s true objective, an agent can find ways to exploit it. Unlike existing surveys that classify reward hacking by where it arises within the alignment pipeline, this paper adopts a different basis and classifies exploitation scenarios by the components of the LLM agent architecture: the language core, memory, the planning module, tools and actions, the observation channel, and the evaluation mechanism. For each component we identify the characteristic exploitation scenarios, the applicable defense methods, and the available benchmarks, which yields a coverage map that exposes threat-defense combinations left uncovered by existing work. We further systematize evaluation metrics by the required level of access to the model, the need for ground-truth annotation, and the need for human judgment, and propose a minimal reporting protocol that makes results comparable across studie

works.title: Reward Hacking in Materials Discovery: An Interpretable Inverse Design Framework and its Physical Limits
works.authors: Aatish Pradhan, Gaurav Vishwakarma, Johannes Hachmann
works.note: ChemRxiv preprint. An inverse-design optimizer produced molecules with a predicted maximum refractive index of 2.16. Independent density-functional calculations capped the index at 1.58.
works.abstract: The inverse design of tailored molecular materials is currently dominated by high-capacity generative models. The “black-box” nature of these models often obscures structure-property relationships and yields candidates with questionable physical transparency. In this work, we present an interpretable, feature-correlation-driven inverse engineering protocol that bridges robust statistical descriptor analysis with constrained genetic algorithms (GAs). By extracting structural primitives via hypergeometric Z-score and A-score analysis-subject to rigorous false discovery rate (FDR) corrections-we provide a physically grounded complement to latent-space sampling. The protocol successfully generated 2nd-generation libraries for high-refractive-index polyimides and high-density organic molecules. Critically, we employ first-principles DFT validation to diagnose the “extrapolation crisis” inherent in 2D surrogate models. The GA successfully optimized topological motifs, yielding a predicted RI max = 2.16 and ρ max = 1770 kg/m^3. DFT validation, however, revealed that 3D steric effects cap the realizable properties at RI = 1.58 and ρ = 1251 kg/m^3. This work establishes a transparent, motif-guided framework for constrained generative design. It also provides a rigorous methodology for identifying the physical boundaries where topological heuristics fail.
works.subcluster: Proxy reward or evaluator rating diverges from task quality

works.title: Preventing Process Reward Model Hacking When Training Large Language Models on Verifiable Rewards
works.authors: Grant C. Forbes, Leonardo Villalobos-Arias, Jianxun Wang, Arnav Jhala, David L. Roberts
works.note: AAMAS extended abstract. Tests when a process reward favors longer, plausible but incorrect reasoning, and studies reward shaping that preserves the optimal policy under the verifiable reward.
works.abstract: Alignment of Large Language Models to human preferences is an active and important field of study. Recent work in Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) aims to bypass the need for costly and imprecise human preference reward data by training LLMs specifically in domains wherein a simple, known solution exists. As the RLVR signal is sparse, however, it is often supplemented with a Process Reward Model (PRM) reward, which provides a dense reward for each token, or step in the chain of thought, for an agent to learn from. Using the VersaPRM extension to the MMLU-Pro dataset, we demonstrate that PRMs are susceptible to reward hacking behavior, wherein the model is incentivized to produce particularly long, plausible-seeming chains of thought that do not result in the correct response. We also develop a theoretical framework and a suite of methods for preventing this reward hacking while still utilizing PRMs effectively, based on recent work in potential-based and optimality-preserving reward shaping. We both prove theoretically and demonstrate practically that these methods prevent PRMs from altering the optimal policy, and thus from being optimized at the expense of the RLVR signal.

works.title: (Some) Natural Emergent Misalignment from Reward Hacking in Non-Production RL
works.authors: Satvik Golechha, Sid Black, Joseph Bloom
works.note: Independent technical report. The team tested the original training design with open models and different coding tasks.

works.title: Competition-Level Code Generation with AlphaCode
works.authors: Yujia Li, David Choi, Junyoung Chung, Nate Kushman, Julian Schrittwieser, Rémi Leblond, Tom Eccles, James Keeling, Felix Gimeno, Agustin Dal Lago, Thomas Hubert, Peter Choy, Cyprien de Masson d'Autume, Igor Babuschkin, Xinyun Chen, Po-Sen Huang, Johannes Welbl, Sven Gowal, Alexey Cherepanov, James Molloy, Daniel J. Mankowitz, Esme Sutherland Robson, Pushmeet Kohli, Nando de Freitas, Koray Kavukcuoglu, Oriol Vinyals
works.abstract: Programming is a powerful and ubiquitous problem-solving tool. Developing systems that can assist programmers or even generate programs independently could make programming more productive and accessible, yet so far incorporating innovations in AI has proven challenging. Recent large-scale language models have demonstrated an impressive ability to generate code, and are now able to complete simple programming tasks. However, these models still perform poorly when evaluated on more complex, unseen problems that require problem-solving skills beyond simply translating instructions into code. For example, competitive programming problems which require an understanding of algorithms and complex natural language remain extremely challenging. To address this gap, we introduce AlphaCode, a system for code generation that can create novel solutions to these problems that require deeper reasoning. In simulated evaluations on recent programming competitions on the Codeforces platform, AlphaCode achieved on average a ranking of top 54.3% in competitions with more than 5,000 participants. We found that three key components were critical to achieve good and reliable performance: (1) an extensive and clean competitive programming dataset for training and evaluation, (2) large and efficient-to-sample transformer-based architectures, and (3) large-scale model sampling to explore the search space, followed by filtering based on program behavior to a small set of submissions.

works.title: Evaluating Interactivity: Toward Automated Assessment of AI-Generated Explorable Explanations
works.authors: Xiaozao Wang, Zhewei Wang, Hongyi Wen
works.abstract: While large language models now enable rapid generation of interactive learning materials, evaluating the interaction quality of these explorable explanations remains an open challenge. Existing benchmarks largely focus on code executability or visual fidelity, providing limited insight into dynamic interaction behaviors such as learner-controlled state transitions and context-sensitive system responses, which are factors that critically shape learners' conceptual understanding. We present EE-Eval, an automated evaluation framework that formalizes interactivity as a finite space of learner-controllable states and transitions, represented as a Finite State Machine (FSM). By extracting FSMs from AI-generated explorable explanations, EE-Eval externalizes implicit interaction logic into an explicit, machine-interpretable graph. Evaluation is performed by comparing each generated FSM to an ideal FSM that encodes pedagogical intent, using a combination of graph-based metrics and embedding-based comparison of states, actions, and feedback to measure their structural and semantic similarity. Across thousands of generated explorable explanations spanning 127 concepts and produced by 6 AI models, EE-Eval consistently differentiates interaction quality beyond surface-level criteria such as functional correctness or visual quality, and exhibits substantially stronger alignment with human judgments of interactivity and pedagogical effectiveness than existing baselines. By framing interactivity as testable behavioral models rather than an emergent byproduct of LLM generation, EE-Eval transforms evaluation into a reflective diagnostic tool, enabling pedagogically grounded and actionable human-AI collaboration in creating interactive educational content.

works.title: LLMs as Factual Reasoners: Insights from Existing Benchmarks and Beyond
works.authors: Philippe Laban, Wojciech Kryściński, Divyansh Agarwal, Alexander R. Fabbri, Caiming Xiong, Shafiq Joty, Chien-Sheng Wu
works.abstract: With the recent appearance of LLMs in practical settings, having methods that can effectively detect factual inconsistencies is crucial to reduce the propagation of misinformation and improve trust in model outputs. When testing on existing factual consistency benchmarks, we find that a few large language models (LLMs) perform competitively on classification benchmarks for factual inconsistency detection compared to traditional non-LLM methods. However, a closer analysis reveals that most LLMs fail on more complex formulations of the task and exposes issues with existing evaluation benchmarks, affecting evaluation precision. To address this, we propose a new protocol for inconsistency detection benchmark creation and implement it in a 10-domain benchmark called SummEdits. This new benchmark is 20 times more cost-effective per sample than previous benchmarks and highly reproducible, as we estimate inter-annotator agreement at about 0.9. Most LLMs struggle on SummEdits, with performance close to random chance. The best-performing model, GPT-4, is still 8\% below estimated human performance, highlighting the gaps in LLMs' ability to reason about facts and detect inconsistencies when they occur.

works.title: RewardBench: Evaluating Reward Models for Language Modeling
works.authors: Nathan Lambert, Valentina Pyatkin, Jacob Morrison, LJ Miranda, Bill Yuchen Lin, Khyathi Chandu, Nouha Dziri, Sachin Kumar, Tom Zick, Yejin Choi, Noah A. Smith, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
works.abstract: Reward models (RMs) are at the crux of successfully using RLHF to align pretrained models to human preferences, yet there has been relatively little study that focuses on evaluation of those models. Evaluating reward models presents an opportunity to understand the opaque technologies used for alignment of language models and which values are embedded in them. Resources for reward model training and understanding are sparse in the nascent open-source community around them. To enhance scientific understanding of reward models, we present RewardBench, a benchmark dataset and code-base for evaluation. The RewardBench dataset is a collection of prompt-chosen-rejected trios spanning chat, reasoning, and safety, to benchmark how reward models perform on challenging, structured and out-of-distribution queries. We create specific comparison datasets for RMs that have subtle, but verifiable reasons (e.g. bugs, incorrect facts) why one answer should be preferred to another. On the RewardBench leaderboard, we evaluate reward models trained with a variety of methods, such as the direct MLE training of classifiers and the implicit reward modeling of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO). We present many findings on propensity for refusals, reasoning limitations, and instruction following shortcomings of various reward models towards a better understanding of the RLHF process.

works.title: InjecGuard: Benchmarking and Mitigating Over-defense in Prompt Injection Guardrail Models
works.authors: Hao Li, Xiaogeng Liu
works.abstract: Prompt injection attacks pose a critical threat to large language models (LLMs), enabling goal hijacking and data leakage. Prompt guard models, though effective in defense, suffer from over-defense -- falsely flagging benign inputs as malicious due to trigger word bias. To address this issue, we introduce NotInject, an evaluation dataset that systematically measures over-defense across various prompt guard models. NotInject contains 339 benign samples enriched with trigger words common in prompt injection attacks, enabling fine-grained evaluation. Our results show that state-of-the-art models suffer from over-defense issues, with accuracy dropping close to random guessing levels (60%). To mitigate this, we propose InjecGuard, a novel prompt guard model that incorporates a new training strategy, Mitigating Over-defense for Free (MOF), which significantly reduces the bias on trigger words. InjecGuard demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on diverse benchmarks including NotInject, surpassing the existing best model by 30.8%, offering a robust and open-source solution for detecting prompt injection attacks. The code and datasets are released at https://github.com/leolee99/InjecGuard.

works.title: Echoes in AI: Quantifying lack of plot diversity in LLM outputs
works.authors: Weijia Xu, Nebojsa Jojic, Sudha Rao, Chris Brockett, Bill Dolan
works.abstract: With rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), there has been an increasing application of LLMs in creative content ideation and generation. A critical question emerges: can current LLMs provide ideas that are diverse enough to truly bolster collective creativity? We examine two state-of-the-art LLMs, GPT-4 and LLaMA-3, on story generation and discover that LLM-generated stories often consist of plot elements that are echoed across a number of generations. To quantify this phenomenon, we introduce the Sui Generis score, an automatic metric that measures the uniqueness of a plot element among alternative storylines generated using the same prompt under an LLM. Evaluating on 100 short stories, we find that LLM-generated stories often contain combinations of idiosyncratic plot elements echoed frequently across generations and across different LLMs, while plots from the original human-written stories are rarely recreated or even echoed in pieces. Moreover, our human evaluation shows that the ranking of Sui Generis scores among story segments correlates moderately with human judgment of surprise level, even though score computation is completely automatic without relying on human judgment.

works.title: Emergent Misalignment: Narrow finetuning can produce broadly misaligned LLMs
works.authors: Jan Betley, Daniel Tan, Niels Warncke, Anna Sztyber-Betley, Xuchan Bao, Martín Soto, Nathan Labenz, Owain Evans
works.abstract: We present a surprising result regarding LLMs and alignment. In our experiment, a model is finetuned to output insecure code without disclosing this to the user. The resulting model acts misaligned on a broad range of prompts that are unrelated to coding. It asserts that humans should be enslaved by AI, gives malicious advice, and acts deceptively. Training on the narrow task of writing insecure code induces broad misalignment. We call this emergent misalignment. This effect is observed in a range of models but is strongest in GPT-4o and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B-Instruct. Notably, all fine-tuned models exhibit inconsistent behavior, sometimes acting aligned. Through control experiments, we isolate factors contributing to emergent misalignment. Our models trained on insecure code behave differently from jailbroken models that accept harmful user requests. Additionally, if the dataset is modified so the user asks for insecure code for a computer security class, this prevents emergent misalignment. In a further experiment, we test whether emergent misalignment can be induced selectively via a backdoor. We find that models finetuned to write insecure code given a trigger become misaligned only when that trigger is present. So the misalignment is hidden without knowledge of the trigger. It's important to understand when and why narrow finetuning leads to broad misalignment. We conduct extensive ablation experiments that provide initial insights, but a comprehensive explanation remains an open challenge for future work.

works.title: A Survey on Video Temporal Grounding with Multimodal Large Language Model
works.authors: Jianlong Wu, Wei Liu, Ye Liu, Meng Liu, Liqiang Nie, Zhouchen Lin, Chang Wen Chen
works.abstract: The recent advancement in video temporal grounding (VTG) has significantly enhanced fine-grained video understanding, primarily driven by multimodal large language models (MLLMs). With superior multimodal comprehension and reasoning abilities, VTG approaches based on MLLMs (VTG-MLLMs) are gradually surpassing traditional fine-tuned methods. They not only achieve competitive performance but also excel in generalization across zero-shot, multi-task, and multi-domain settings. Despite extensive surveys on general video-language understanding, comprehensive reviews specifically addressing VTG-MLLMs remain scarce. To fill this gap, this survey systematically examines current research on VTG-MLLMs through a three-dimensional taxonomy: 1) the functional roles of MLLMs, highlighting their architectural significance; 2) training paradigms, analyzing strategies for temporal reasoning and task adaptation; and 3) video feature processing techniques, which determine spatiotemporal representation effectiveness. We further discuss benchmark datasets, evaluation protocols, and summarize empirical findings. Finally, we identify existing limitations and propose promising research directions. For additional resources and details, readers are encouraged to visit our repository at https://github.com/ki-lw/Awesome-MLLMs-for-Video-Temporal-Grounding.

works.title: AI Deception: A Survey of Examples, Risks, and Potential Solutions
works.authors: Peter S. Park, Simon Goldstein, Aidan O'Gara, Michael Chen, Dan Hendrycks
works.abstract: This paper argues that a range of current AI systems have learned how to deceive humans. We define deception as the systematic inducement of false beliefs in the pursuit of some outcome other than the truth. We first survey empirical examples of AI deception, discussing both special-use AI systems (including Meta's CICERO) built for specific competitive situations, and general-purpose AI systems (such as large language models). Next, we detail several risks from AI deception, such as fraud, election tampering, and losing control of AI systems. Finally, we outline several potential solutions to the problems posed by AI deception: first, regulatory frameworks should subject AI systems that are capable of deception to robust risk-assessment requirements; second, policymakers should implement bot-or-not laws; and finally, policymakers should prioritize the funding of relevant research, including tools to detect AI deception and to make AI systems less deceptive. Policymakers, researchers, and the broader public should work proactively to prevent AI deception from destabilizing the shared foundations of our society.

works.title: A practical identifiability criterion leveraging weak-form parameter estimation
works.authors: Nora Heitzman-Breen, Vanja Dukic, David M. Bortz
works.abstract: In this work, we define a practical identifiability criterion, (e, q)-identifiability, based on a parameter e, reflecting the noise in observed variables, and a parameter q, reflecting the mean-square error of the parameter estimator. This criterion is better able to encompass changes in the quality of the parameter estimate due to increased noise in the data (compared to existing criteria based solely on average relative errors). Furthermore, we leverage a weak-form equation error-based method of parameter estimation for systems with unobserved variables to assess practical identifiability far more quickly in comparison to output error-based parameter estimation. We do so by generating weak-form input-output equations using differential algebra techniques, as previously proposed by Boulier et al [1], and then applying Weak form Estimation of Nonlinear Dynamics (WENDy) to obtain parameter estimates. This method is computationally efficient and robust to noise, as demonstrated through two classical biological modelling examples.

works.title: Asymptotic consistency of the WSINDy algorithm in the limit of continuum data
works.authors: Daniel A. Messenger, David M. Bortz
works.abstract: In this work we study the asymptotic consistency of the weak-form sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics algorithm (WSINDy) in the identification of differential equations from noisy samples of solutions. We prove that the WSINDy estimator is unconditionally asymptotically consistent for a wide class of models which includes the Navier-Stokes equations and the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation. We thus provide a mathematically rigorous explanation for the observed robustness to noise of weak-form equation learning. Conversely, we also show that in general the WSINDy estimator is only conditionally asymptotically consistent, yielding discovery of spurious terms with probability one if the noise level is above some critical threshold and the nonlinearities exhibit sufficiently fast growth. We derive explicit bounds on the critical noise threshold in the case of Gaussian white noise and provide an explicit characterization of these spurious terms in the case of trigonometric and/or polynomial model nonlinearities. However, a silver lining to this negative result is that if the data is suitably denoised (a simple moving average filter is sufficient), then we recover unconditional asymptotic consistency on the class of models with locally-Lipschitz nonlinearities. Altogether, our results reveal several important aspects of weak-form equation learning which may be used to improve future algorithms. We demonstrate our results numerically using the Lorenz system, the cubic oscillator, a viscous Burgers growth model, and a Kuramoto-Sivashinsky-type higher-order PDE.

works.title: Weak Form Scientific Machine Learning: Test Function Construction for System Identification
works.authors: April Tran, David Bortz
works.abstract:
Weak form Scientific Machine Learning (WSciML) is a recently developed framework for data-driven modeling and scientific discovery. It leverages the weak form of equation error residuals to provide enhanced noise robustness in system identification via convolving model equations with test functions, reformulating the problem to avoid direct differentiation of data. The performance, however, relies on wisely choosing a set of compactly supported test functions.
 In this work, we mathematically motivate a novel data-driven method for constructing Single-scale-Local reference functions for creating the set of test functions. Our approach numerically approximates the integration error introduced by the quadrature and identifies the support size for which the error is minimal, without requiring access to the model parameter values. Through numerical experiments across various models, noise levels, and temporal resolutions, we demonstrate that the selected supports consistently align with regions of minimal parameter estimation error. We also compare the proposed method against the strategy for constructing Multi-scale-Global (and orthogonal) test functions introduced in our prior work, demonstrating the improved computational efficiency.

works.title: Agent Incentives: A Causal Perspective
works.authors: Tom Everitt, Ryan Carey, Eric Langlois, Pedro A Ortega, Shane Legg
works.abstract: We present a framework for analysing agent incentives using causal influence diagrams. We establish that a well-known criterion for value of information is complete. We propose a new graphical criterion for value of control, establishing its soundness and completeness. We also introduce two new concepts for incentive analysis: response incentives indicate which changes in the environment affect an optimal decision, while instrumental control incentives establish whether an agent can influence its utility via a variable X. For both new concepts, we provide sound and complete graphical criteria. We show by example how these results can help with evaluating the safety and fairness of an AI system.

works.title: Artificial Intelligence, Values and Alignment
works.authors: Iason Gabriel
works.abstract: This paper looks at philosophical questions that arise in the context of AI alignment. It defends three propositions. First, normative and technical aspects of the AI alignment problem are interrelated, creating space for productive engagement between people working in both domains. Second, it is important to be clear about the goal of alignment. There are significant differences between AI that aligns with instructions, intentions, revealed preferences, ideal preferences, interests and values. A principle-based approach to AI alignment, which combines these elements in a systematic way, has considerable advantages in this context. Third, the central challenge for theorists is not to identify 'true' moral principles for AI; rather, it is to identify fair principles for alignment, that receive reflective endorsement despite widespread variation in people's moral beliefs. The final part of the paper explores three ways in which fair principles for AI alignment could potentially be identified.

works.title: Reward-rational (implicit) choice: A unifying formalism for reward learning
works.authors: Hong Jun Jeon, Smitha Milli, Anca D. Dragan
works.abstract: It is often difficult to hand-specify what the correct reward function is for a task, so researchers have instead aimed to learn reward functions from human behavior or feedback. The types of behavior interpreted as evidence of the reward function have expanded greatly in recent years. We've gone from demonstrations, to comparisons, to reading into the information leaked when the human is pushing the robot away or turning it off. And surely, there is more to come. How will a robot make sense of all these diverse types of behavior? Our key insight is that different types of behavior can be interpreted in a single unifying formalism - as a reward-rational choice that the human is making, often implicitly. The formalism offers both a unifying lens with which to view past work, as well as a recipe for interpreting new sources of information that are yet to be uncovered. We provide two examples to showcase this: interpreting a new feedback type, and reading into how the choice of feedback itself leaks information about the reward.

works.title: REALab: An Embedded Perspective on Tampering
works.authors: Ramana Kumar, Jonathan Uesato, Richard Ngo, Tom Everitt, Victoria Krakovna, Shane Legg
works.abstract: This paper describes REALab, a platform for embedded agency research in reinforcement learning (RL). REALab is designed to model the structure of tampering problems that may arise in real-world deployments of RL. Standard Markov Decision Process (MDP) formulations of RL and simulated environments mirroring the MDP structure assume secure access to feedback (e.g., rewards). This may be unrealistic in settings where agents are embedded and can corrupt the processes producing feedback (e.g., human supervisors, or an implemented reward function). We describe an alternative Corrupt Feedback MDP formulation and the REALab environment platform, which both avoid the secure feedback assumption. We hope the design of REALab provides a useful perspective on tampering problems, and that the platform may serve as a unit test for the presence of tampering incentives in RL agent designs.

works.title: Offline Reinforcement Learning: Tutorial, Review, and Perspectives on Open Problems
works.authors: Sergey Levine, Aviral Kumar, George Tucker, Justin Fu
works.abstract: In this tutorial article, we aim to provide the reader with the conceptual tools needed to get started on research on offline reinforcement learning algorithms: reinforcement learning algorithms that utilize previously collected data, without additional online data collection. Offline reinforcement learning algorithms hold tremendous promise for making it possible to turn large datasets into powerful decision making engines. Effective offline reinforcement learning methods would be able to extract policies with the maximum possible utility out of the available data, thereby allowing automation of a wide range of decision-making domains, from healthcare and education to robotics. However, the limitations of current algorithms make this difficult. We will aim to provide the reader with an understanding of these challenges, particularly in the context of modern deep reinforcement learning methods, and describe some potential solutions that have been explored in recent work to mitigate these challenges, along with recent applications, and a discussion of perspectives on open problems in the field.

works.title: From Optimizing Engagement to Measuring Value
works.authors: Smitha Milli, Luca Belli, Moritz Hardt
works.abstract: Most recommendation engines today are based on predicting user engagement, e.g. predicting whether a user will click on an item or not. However, there is potentially a large gap between engagement signals and a desired notion of "value" that is worth optimizing for. We use the framework of measurement theory to (a) confront the designer with a normative question about what the designer values, (b) provide a general latent variable model approach that can be used to operationalize the target construct and directly optimize for it, and (c) guide the designer in evaluating and revising their operationalization. We implement our approach on the Twitter platform on millions of users. In line with established approaches to assessing the validity of measurements, we perform a qualitative evaluation of how well our model captures a desired notion of "value".

works.title: The EMPATHIC Framework for Task Learning from Implicit Human Feedback
works.authors: Yuchen Cui, Qiping Zhang, Alessandro Allievi, Peter Stone, Scott Niekum, W. Bradley Knox
works.abstract: Reactions such as gestures, facial expressions, and vocalizations are an abundant, naturally occurring channel of information that humans provide during interactions. A robot or other agent could leverage an understanding of such implicit human feedback to improve its task performance at no cost to the human. This approach contrasts with common agent teaching methods based on demonstrations, critiques, or other guidance that need to be attentively and intentionally provided. In this paper, we first define the general problem of learning from implicit human feedback and then propose to address this problem through a novel data-driven framework, EMPATHIC. This two-stage method consists of (1) mapping implicit human feedback to relevant task statistics such as reward, optimality, and advantage; and (2) using such a mapping to learn a task. We instantiate the first stage and three second-stage evaluations of the learned mapping. To do so, we collect a dataset of human facial reactions while participants observe an agent execute a sub-optimal policy for a prescribed training task. We train a deep neural network on this data and demonstrate its ability to (1) infer relative reward ranking of events in the training task from prerecorded human facial reactions; (2) improve the policy of an agent in the training task using live human facial reactions; and (3) transfer to a novel domain in which it evaluates robot manipulation trajectories.

works.title: Words aren't enough, their order matters: On the Robustness of Grounding Visual Referring Expressions
works.authors: Arjun R Akula, Spandana Gella, Yaser Al-Onaizan, Song-Chun Zhu, Siva Reddy
works.abstract: Visual referring expression recognition is a challenging task that requires natural language understanding in the context of an image.
